name: OpenSpec
description: Spec-driven development (SDD) for AI coding assistants.
readmeExcerpt:
The most loved spec framework.

Our philosophy: ```text → fluid not rigid → iterative not waterfall → easy not complex → built for brownfield not just greenfield → scalable from personal projects to enterprises ```

Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions.

## See it in action ```text You: /opsx:explore AI: What would you like to explore? You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly. AI: Let me look at your styling setup... Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context, with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it? You: Yes, let's do it. You: /opsx:propose add-dark-mode AI: Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/ ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing ✓ specs/ — requirements and scenarios ✓ design.md — technical approach ✓ tasks.md — implementation checklist Ready for implementation! You: /opsx:apply AI: Implementing tasks... ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage All tasks complete! You: /opsx:archive AI: Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/ Specs updated. Ready for the next feature. ```
What do the specs actually look like? Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the `specs/` folder created above: ```markdown ## ADDED Requirements ### Requirement: Theme selection The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes, defaulting to the system preference. #### Scenario: User toggles dark mode - **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle - **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice ``` Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written. OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live [specs](openspec/specs) and in-flight [changes](openspec/changes) for real examples at scale.
OpenSpec Dashboard

## Why teams adopt OpenSpec Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists. **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)** are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same `openspec/` shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by `git push` like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo. - **Cross-repo features** — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos. - **Shared requirements** — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki. - **Plan before code** — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later. > Stores are in **beta**. Start with the [Stores guide](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores). ## Quick Start Install OpenSpec. It is a single file and needs no Node.js (on Alpine Linux, first run `apk add libstdc++ libgcc`). macOS and Linux: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/main/scripts/binary/install.sh | sh ``` Windows (PowerShell): ```powershell irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/main/scripts/binary/install.ps1 | iex ``` Prefer a package manager? `npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest` (needs Node.js 20.19.0 or higher) or the official [Homebrew formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/openspec), `brew install openspec`. Then navigate to your project directory and initialize: ```bash cd your-project openspec init ``` > **Want your AI to do it?** Paste the [setup prompt](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation#install-with-your-ai-assistant) into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs `openspec init`, and verifies the result. Now talk to your AI: - **Not sure what to build yet?** Start with `/opsx:explore`, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. ([Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)) - **Already know what you want?** Go straight to `/opsx:propose `. Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (`/opsx:new`, `/opsx:continue`, `/opsx:ff`, `/opsx:verify`, `/opsx:bulk-archive`, `/opsx:onboard`), select it with `openspec config profile` and apply with `openspec update`. `/opsx:propose` is the canonical name; your tool may spell it `/opsx-propose` (Cursor, GitHub Copilot), `@opsx-propose` (Amazon Q) or `$openspec-propose` (Codex). `openspec init` prints the right form for the tools you picked — see [Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools). > [!NOTE] > Not sure if your tool is supported? [View the full list](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools) – we support 30+ tools and growing. > > Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. [See installation options](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation). ## Docs Full documentation lives at **[openspec.dev/docs](https://openspec.dev/docs)**. → **[Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)**: your first change, start to finish
→ **[Set up your project](https://openspec.dev/docs/setup)**: what `openspec init` installs
→ **[CLI](https://openspec.dev/docs/cli)**: terminal reference
→ **[Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools)**: tool integrations & install paths
→ **[Customize](https://openspec.dev/docs/customize)**: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)**: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ **[Community Showcase](docs/community.md)**: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec ## Community schemas Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how [github/spec-kit's community extension catalog](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/tree/main/extensions) handles tool integrations. → **[Browse the catalog](docs/customization.md#community-schemas)** in the customization docs. ## Why OpenSpec? AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written. - **Agree before you build** — human and AI align on specs before code gets written - **Stay organized** — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks - **Work fluidly** — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates - **Use your tools** — works with 30+ AI assistants via slash commands ### How we compare **vs. [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit)** (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely. **vs. [Kiro](https://kiro.dev)** (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use. **vs. nothing** — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony. ## Updating OpenSpec **Upgrade the CLI** With the standalone install, run `openspec install`. If you installed with npm: ```bash npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest ``` If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew: ```bash brew upgrade openspec ``` **Refresh agent instructions** Run this inside each project to regenerate AI guidance and ensure the latest slash commands are active: ```bash openspec update ``` ## Usage Notes **Model selection**: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation. **Context hygiene**: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session. ## Contributing Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us. → **[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)**: the full process, from first issue to merged PR ## Other
Telemetry OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats. We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI. **Opt-out (any one is enough):** - `openspec config set telemetry.enabled false` (global config; unset means on) - `export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0` or `export DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors See [MAINTAINERS.md](MAINTAINERS.md) for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.
## License MIT

releases.name: v1.15.0 - Standalone install, update dry run
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.15.0

You can now install OpenSpec without Node.js, using one command, and `openspec update` can now show what it would change before changing anything.

### New

- **Standalone install** - Install OpenSpec with one command and no Node.js: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/main/scripts/binary/install.sh | sh` on macOS and Linux, or `irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/main/scripts/binary/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows. Every release now ships binaries for macOS, Linux (glibc and musl) and Windows on x64 and arm64, with `SHA256SUMS`. npm and the other package managers keep working as before.
- **`openspec update --dry-run`** - Reports the files an update would add, change or delete without writing anything; add `--json` for machine-readable output.

### Improved

- **Faster `--json` commands** - `status`, `instructions`, `new change`, `templates`, `validate` and `schema` no longer load the spinner package when run with `--json`, so they start a little faster. Output is unchanged.
- **`openspec feedback`** - Filed issues now match the bug form, and the manual-submission link opens the bug form with y

releases.name: v1.14.3 - Clean audits, safer globs
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.14.3

This release removes a dependency that kept failing security audits, fixes a validate hang in pre-commit hooks, and stops refusing some symlinked spec files.

### Improved

- **No more `braces` audit warning** - Installing OpenSpec no longer pulls in the unpatched `braces` package, so `npm audit` in your project stops reporting GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm through OpenSpec.
- **Glob artifacts stay inside the change** - The propose, ff, continue and explore workflows now choose and check a glob artifact's file path before anything writes it, including a skill or command the schema delegates creation to. A path that would leave the change directory, directly or through a symlink, is refused.

### Fixed

- **Symlinked spec files no longer refused** - `list --specs`, `show`, `validate` and `archive` no longer error out when a capability's `spec.md` is a symlink inside the project. Symlinked layouts are not officially supported. A link that resolves outside the project is still refused.
- **`validate --all` hanging in hooks** - On a terminal that reports zero columns, as some pre-commit runners provide, the spinner no longer loops forever writing cursor escapes. `OPEN_S

releases.name: v1.14.2 - Faster completion and fixes
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.14.2

This release makes Tab completion faster and closes gaps where archive and verify could lose or miss content.

### Improved

- **Faster Tab completion** - Shell completion now loads 48 modules instead of 344 when completing changes or specs, and no longer records usage, so a Tab press never waits on telemetry.
- **Warnings for text archive drops** - `openspec validate` and `openspec archive` now warn when a delta spec holds text that archive does not carry into the main spec, such as an extra `## ` section or prose before the first requirement. Like other warnings, these fail `openspec validate --strict`.
- **Verify checks removed requirements properly** - `/opsx:verify` reads a REMOVED requirement's original text from the main spec before searching the code, and reports the entry as not verified when that text cannot be recovered, instead of passing it.

### Fixed

- **`x-` keys in `.openspec.yaml` no longer fail validation** - `openspec validate --strict` no longer reports top-level keys starting with a lowercase `x-`; OpenSpec ignores them. This is not an officially supported extension mechanism. Any other unrecognized key is still reported.

releases.name: v1.14.1 - Faster startup, cleaner view
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.14.1

This release starts the CLI faster, keeps archived changes off the `openspec view` dashboard, and makes spec writing, verify, and archive more reliable.

### Improved

- **Faster startup** - Each command loads only the code it needs, so `openspec --version` and `--help` load 24 modules instead of 485. The difference is largest on Windows.
- **Spec writing** - Agents write each capability's spec file as soon as it is drafted instead of planning every file first, so long runs show progress and an interrupted run keeps the files it wrote. `/opsx:continue` writes any specs still missing before moving on.
- **Strict requirement length** - A requirement over 500 characters is now a warning, so `openspec validate --strict` fails on it, including new requirements in a change.

### Fixed

- **`openspec view`** - The dashboard no longer lists or counts archived changes. `openspec list --archived` still shows them.
- **Verify with custom schemas** - `/opsx:verify` finds spec and design artifacts by their output path, so it works when a schema names those artifacts differently.
- **Apply completion** - When every tracked task is checked, apply says the tasks are compl

releases.name: v1.14.0 - Ten new tools, archived changes
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.14.0

This release adds ten new tools, lets you browse archived changes, and makes apply, archive, and store-backed changes more reliable.

### New

- **Ten new tools** - `openspec init` and `openspec update` now support Amp (`amp`), AtomCode (`atomcode`), Code Studio (`codestudio`), DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`), EasyCode (`easycode`), GigaCode (`gigacode`), Grok Build (`grok`), GSD (`gsd`), Veai (`veai`), and Warp (`warp`).
- **Archived changes** - `openspec list --archived` and `--all` list archived changes, with JSON output and sorting, and `openspec view` shows them in their own section.
- **Workflow status in `openspec view`** - The dashboard shows each active change's schema and which artifacts are done, ready, blocked, or skipped.
- **`openspec version`** - Shows the installed version and install type. Add `--check` and `--json` for structured update information that tools can read.
- **Nix overlay** - The flake exposes OpenSpec through `overlays.default`, so other flakes can consume it.

### Improved

- **Unrecognized change metadata** - `status`, `validate`, and `archive` now name keys in `.openspec.yaml` that OpenSpec ignores, such as `skip_design`, instea

readmeHtml:
The most loved spec framework.

Our philosophy: 
→ fluid not rigid
→ iterative not waterfall
→ easy not complex
→ built for brownfield not just greenfield
→ scalable from personal projects to enterprises

Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions.

See it in action

You: /opsx:explore
AI:  What would you like to explore?
You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly.
AI:  Let me look at your styling setup...
     Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context,
     with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it?
You: Yes, let's do it.

You: /opsx:propose add-dark-mode
AI:  Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/
     ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing
     ✓ specs/       — requirements and scenarios
     ✓ design.md    — technical approach
     ✓ tasks.md     — implementation checklist
     Ready for implementation!

You: /opsx:apply
AI:  Implementing tasks...
     ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider
     ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component
     ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables
     ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage
     All tasks complete!

You: /opsx:archive
AI:  Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/
     Specs updated. Ready for the next feature.
What do the specs actually look like?

Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the specs/ folder created above:

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Theme selection
The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes,
defaulting to the system preference.

#### Scenario: User toggles dark mode
- **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle
- **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice

Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written.

OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live specs and in-flight changes for real examples at scale.

OpenSpec Dashboard

Why teams adopt OpenSpec

Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists.

Stores are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same openspec/ shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by git push like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo.

  • Cross-repo features — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos.
  • Shared requirements — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki.
  • Plan before code — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later.

Stores are in beta. Start with the Stores guide.

Quick Start

Install OpenSpec. It is a single file and needs no Node.js (on Alpine Linux, first run apk add libstdc++ libgcc).

macOS and Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/main/scripts/binary/install.sh | sh

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/main/scripts/binary/install.ps1 | iex

Prefer a package manager? npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest (needs Node.js 20.19.0 or higher) or the official Homebrew formula, brew install openspec.

Then navigate to your project directory and initialize:

cd your-project
openspec init

Want your AI to do it? Paste the setup prompt into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs openspec init, and verifies the result.

Now talk to your AI:

  • Not sure what to build yet? Start with /opsx:explore, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. (Quickstart)
  • Already know what you want? Go straight to /opsx:propose <what-you-want-to-build>.

Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (/opsx:new, /opsx:continue, /opsx:ff, /opsx:verify, /opsx:bulk-archive, /opsx:onboard), select it with openspec config profile and apply with openspec update.

/opsx:propose is the canonical name; your tool may spell it /opsx-propose (Cursor, GitHub Copilot), @opsx-propose (Amazon Q) or $openspec-propose (Codex). openspec init prints the right form for the tools you picked — see Supported Tools.

Note

Not sure if your tool is supported? View the full list – we support 30+ tools and growing.

Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. See installation options.

Docs

Full documentation lives at openspec.dev/docs.

→ Quickstart: your first change, start to finish
→ Set up your project: what openspec init installs
→ CLI: terminal reference
→ Supported Tools: tool integrations & install paths
→ Customize: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ Stores: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ Community Showcase: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec

Community schemas

Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how github/spec-kit's community extension catalog handles tool integrations.

→ Browse the catalog in the customization docs.

Why OpenSpec?

AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written.

  • Agree before you build — human and AI align on specs before code gets written
  • Stay organized — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks
  • Work fluidly — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates
  • Use your tools — works with 30+ AI assistants via slash commands

How we compare

vs. Spec Kit (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely.

vs. Kiro (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use.

vs. nothing — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony.

Updating OpenSpec

Upgrade the CLI

With the standalone install, run openspec install. If you installed with npm:

npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest

If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew:

brew upgrade openspec

Refresh agent instructions

Run this inside each project to regenerate AI guidance and ensure the latest slash commands are active:

openspec update

Usage Notes

Model selection: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation.

Context hygiene: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session.

Contributing

Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us.

→ CONTRIBUTING.md: the full process, from first issue to merged PR

Other

Telemetry

OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats.

We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI.

Opt-out (any one is enough):

  • openspec config set telemetry.enabled false (global config; unset means on)
  • export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 or export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors

See MAINTAINERS.md for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.

License

MIT

aiSummary.oneLiner: A spec-driven development framework promoting fluid and iterative software specifications for AI coding assistants.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: OpenSpec introduces an iterative spec-driven development methodology tailored for modern AI coding assistants. The framework replaces rigid waterfall planning with an artifact-guided workflow that remains fluid and easily adaptable throughout the software development lifecycle. By utilizing context engineering, the tool enables AI agents to better understand and act upon software design documents and product requirements. This approach scales seamlessly from small personal tools to large enterprise architectures, specifically accommodating brownfield projects rather than just greenfield deployments.
keyFeatures: Iterative specification: Promotes fluid and adaptable software design documents rather than rigid waterfall planning.
AI assistant integration: Tailors product requirements and system architecture documents specifically for AI agents to process.
Artifact-guided workflow: Uses structured artifacts to direct the software development lifecycle effectively.
Brownfield support: Adapts seamlessly to existing legacy codebases rather than solely focusing on new greenfield projects.
Scalable architecture: Handles varying project complexities from individual developer tools to comprehensive enterprise systems.

useCases.title: Guiding AI coding assistants
useCases.description: Write structured specifications that help AI agents understand the complete architecture before generating code.

useCases.title: Managing complex requirements
useCases.description: Maintain fluid product requirements that can evolve dynamically as project assumptions change.

useCases.title: Documenting brownfield architectures
useCases.description: Generate clear architectural specifications for existing legacy systems to assist new developers or AI tools.

useCases.title: Standardizing team planning
useCases.description: Implement a unified specification framework to streamline planning phases across large engineering teams.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: This framework is targeted at software architects, technical product managers, and developers utilizing AI coding assistants. It serves engineering teams that require structured, yet flexible, methodologies to guide complex software development.
